questions.question: How does FastText handle out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words differently than Word2Vec?
options: It represents a word as a sum of its character n-grams.
It skips the word and moves to the next one.
It assigns a random vector to any unknown word.
It uses a dictionary lookup to find the closest synonym.
questions.explanation: FastText breaks words into character n-grams (e.g., 'where' -> '<wh', 'whe', 'her'...). Even if the full word was never seen, its sub-parts likely were, allowing the model to construct a vector for the new word.

questions.question: What is the core idea behind Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE)?
options: Iteratively merging the most frequent adjacent character or subword pairs.
Encrypting words into bytes for security.
Using only 256 tokens for the entire vocabulary.
Sorting the vocabulary by byte size.
questions.explanation: BPE starts with characters/bytes and merges the most frequent adjacent units into larger subword tokens, creating a vocabulary that balances common words and rare pieces.

questions.question: Why is GloVe often considered 'global' compared to Word2Vec's 'local' approach?
options: It factorizes a global co-occurrence matrix instead of doing local window updates.
It was trained on the entire internet at once.
It uses coordinates from a global map for embeddings.
It works on all languages without modification.
questions.explanation: Word2Vec scans the corpus in a sliding window (local). GloVe first compiles a corpus-wide word-word co-occurrence matrix (global) and then factorizes it.

questions.question: Which tokenization method is the most common choice for modern Large Language Models (LLMs) as of 2026?
questions.explanation: Subword tokenization is the standard for LLMs like GPT, BERT, and LLaMA because it provides a fixed-size vocabulary that can represent any possible string without 'out-of-vocabulary' errors.
